newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Darling reaffirms savings pledges.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Darling reaffirms savings pledges.

text.p: Alistair Darling, the opposition Labour Party's shadow chief secretary at the UK Treasury, re-affirmed the Party's commitment to give tax incentives for long-term savings and to streamline insurance regulations.
Darling told delegates at an insurance industry conference in Newcastle that a Labour government "would ensure appropriate fiscal incentives to encourage long term savings, such as life insurance."

He declined to make any solid promises on tax, but said he recognised the imbalance in tax treatment between life insurance on one hand and personal equity plans (PEPs) and tax exempt savings deposits (TESSAs) on the other, and reiterated his party's opinion that it is right to use tax benefits for such a goal.

He added that Labour wants to simplify regulation of the insurance and financial sectors under the Securities and Investments Board, which would oversee the work of certain other self-regulating authorities.
The proposal follows a series of problems in parts of the UK financial sector in recent years involving the mis-selling of pensions in the UK and difficulties at Lloyd's of London insurance market.
"The current system is confusing and does not lead to public confidence," Darling told delegates at the Chartered Insurance Institute conference in Newcastle.

"We don't want to put the job into the hands of civil servants or politicians - we aim to have a blend of public and professional interest. We want to promote a new professionalism - that is where the future of this industry lies."
Darling added that although it might be difficult to bring in regulatory and tax changes at the same time, he hoped both could be done reasonably close to each other.
His appearance at the conference was the latest in a series of measures aimed at winning confidence from the financial sector that a Labour government would not be bad for business.

Asked by one insurer about his views on European monetary union, Darling said: "We have no difficulty with the idea of a single currency, but whether or not this country joins must depend on whether there is a sustainable economic convergence. We have to be absolutely sure that the structures set up are going to work."
